papers.title: BCell-Epitope-Prediction: A local, reproducible pipeline for multi-epitope vaccine design: integration and structural validation against a panel of PDB antigen-antibody complexes
papers.abstract: Epitope-based subunit vaccine design requires chaining together heterogeneous analyses: B-cell antigenicity, topological accessibility, self-tolerance, allergenicity, T-helper/T-cytotoxic immunogenicity, and literature corroboration, historically scattered across separate, often web-only tools. This work presents a computational pipeline that integrates fourteen external tools across eight main phases, runs locally without network calls, and uses content-based self-caching. B-cell antigenicity is assessed via four engines (BepiPred-3.0, EpiDope, DiscoTope-3.0, and ScanNet), whose per-residue scores are fused into a single signal before thresholding. Validation used a panel of seventeen real antigen-antibody complexes from the Protein Data Bank spanning five pathogenic species, with ground truth from structural contact and independent literature verification. Fusing the four engines' scores, completed to a fixed candidate count, outperforms the best individual engine in F1 while reducing predicted residue volume. T-helper and T-cytotoxic immunogenicity are evaluated over each antigen's complete sequence, independently of the B-cell candidates. The final construct retains a B-cell epitope in 13 of 17 structures, and a T-cell block in 13 of 17 antigens, of which 6 match literature-documented epitopes and 2 more show partial correspondence.

papers.title: VesperFlow: An automated pipeline for decoding multisensor data from biologging tags
papers.abstract: Integrating multi-sensor data from biologging tags is key to understanding animal behavior, particularly in group-living species, where communication, movement, and spatial dynamics are closely linked. However, analyzing such data at scale is often hindered by proprietary binary formats or manual decoding workflows in existing software. We present VesperFlow, an open-source Python pipeline that automates the decoding of inertial measurement unit (IMU), audio, and GPS data from Vesper Wildlife tags. VesperFlow batch-processes large datasets from multiple individuals, synchronizes timestamps across sensors with sub-second precision, and removes hardware-induced artifacts such as spurious gyroscope spikes and audio pops. Outputs are exported as CSV and WAV files for direct use in common downstream analysis workflows. We validate the pipeline on field data from 10 ring-tailed lemurs (Lemur catta), showing that our pipeline reliably processes movement, vocal, and spatial data. By lowering technical barriers and automating processes, VesperFlow supports more scalable, multi-modal research on animal behavior. VesperFlow is freely available at https://github.com/dasilva98/vesperflow.

papers.title: Lack of adoption of computational gene-panel-selection tools in targeted spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Targeted spatial transcriptomics requires selecting a gene panel before any experiment is run. Choosing well across tens of thousands of candidate genes under platform-specific probe, panel-size, and sensitivity constraints is difficult to do manually, and impossible to correct once a panel has been used. A growing number of computational tools to automate this selection have been designed, yet it remains unclear whether they are adopted in practice. Several factors could limit uptake: validation uncertainty about panel performance, workflow friction between a ranked gene list and a submission-ready panel, limited platform awareness in tools developed for dissociated single-cell data, and the cost advantage of vendor panels. We analyzed 18 computational tools for gene-panel selection from two angles: their citation landscape and their use across a targeted spatial transcriptomics corpus. Across 540 full-text-classified records, only 35 (6.5%) reported using the cited tool for panel design; most came from computational, benchmark, review, or non-spatial papers, or papers that cited but did not use it. In an independent corpus, only 34 of 479 (7.1%) involved a computational tool, alone or in a hybrid workflow; most used manually curated, premade vendor, or modified vendor panels. Both lines of evidence point the same way: computational selection is rarely part of the reported experimental workflow, and it more often supplemented manual curation than replaced it. Adoption is unlikely to turn on further benchmark gains alone; it will depend on reducing the validation uncertainty and workflow friction that keep users on established panel-design practice.

papers.title: ALBIS: simulation of multi-resolution and multi-dimensional spatial transcriptomics data
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies has been accompanied by substantial growth in computational methods, creating an increasing need for systematic and reliable benchmarking, particularly as analyses increasingly extend from individual tissue sections to three-dimensional (3D) tissue reconstruction. Existing benchmarks often rely on a small and similar set of experimentally-derived datasets because they offer a reliable ground truth label, which is hard to find in practice. Simulated or synthetic data provide an alternative, yet most existing simulators either adapt single-cell RNA-sequencing models to spatial coordinates or generate individual sections in a two-dimensional (2D) space at predefined resolutions. More recent approaches can simulate 2D and 3D tissues, but generally do not derive multiple spatial resolutions from the same molecular realization. Here, we introduce ALBIS (A muLti-resolution Biological In-silico Simulator for spatial transcriptomics), a statistically grounded and highly customizable framework that generates synthetic ST data from an in silico 3D tissue. ALBIS defines spatially structured cell populations with corresponding markers for gene expression, then initializes individual mRNA molecules in 3D space to create cell-level information with a ground truth 3D coordinate for each molecule and cell. From this common realization, ALBIS cuts the 3D tissue into multiple 2D tissue sections with cell-, bin-, and spot-level measurements, enabling direct comparison across spatial resolutions. Properties of the simulated data, including spatial domains, cell type composition, gene-expression effects, batch effects, measurement resolution, and tissue scale, can be systematically varied, enabling rigorous stress-testing of computational methods under known and increasingly challenging conditions.

papers.title: Pan-cancer estimation of prognostic immune biomarkers from histopathology using artificial intelligence
papers.abstract: Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) assays such as ImmunoProfile provide standardized quantification of prognostic immune markers but are costly and not routinely used in clinical settings. We developed a weakly-supervised AI model, HistoProfile, to estimate intratumoral cell densities of key immune biomarkers (CD8, FOXP3, PD-1, and PD-L1) and the PD-L1 tumor proportion score from routine H&E-stained whole-slide images. Trained on a large pan-cancer cohort with paired H&E and mIF data, HistoProfile discriminated biomarker-high from biomarker-low tumors in held-out samples and tumor-specific subgroups (AUROCs of 0.78-0.89 across biomarkers). Critically, the estimated biomarkers preserved prognostic stratification in downstream survival analyses, and showed cancer-specific survival associations across TCGA cohorts where mIF is unavailable. These findings support scalable H&E-based estimation of key immune biomarker measurements for large-scale immune profiling and risk stratification.

papers.title: Ontology-Driven Annotation of Key Events Enables Transcriptomics-Based Assessment of Adverse Outcome Pathway Networks
papers.abstract: Chemical safety assessment is moving towards new approach methodologies (NAMs) to improve human safety and reduce animal testing. The Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) is a NAM framework describing toxicity as a chain of Key Events (KEs). Many AOP-Wiki KEs describe molecular, cellular, or tissue-level processes and can therefore be assessed with gene expression data, making transcriptomics of human in vitro models a NAM data generator. In AOP-Wiki, KEs are described by Key Event Components (KECs). A gene set can be derived when the biological process (BP) component carries a Gene Ontology (GO) term. Most KEs carry no such term, so their perturbation cannot be assessed using omics data. We assigned GO BP terms to the unmapped BP component across the brain, lung, liver and kidney AOP networks. We also replaced obsolete and direction-carrying terms in the pre-existing mapping with current, direction-neutral ones. For liver, we reviewed all pre-existing terms and replaced overly broad terms with better-matched alternatives. We then applied this approach to pesticide-induced hepatotoxicity, using Open TG-GATEs transcriptomics data from primary human hepatocytes exposed to cycloheximide, 2,4-dinitrophenol, hexachlorobenzene, and rotenone. KE perturbation was scored using single-sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (ssGSEA). Annotation increased the proportion of transcriptomics-linkable KEs in the liver network from 53% to 77%, enhancing identification of perturbed KEs after exposure. The KEs perturbed by all four compounds fell into five functional categories associated with hepatotoxicity. Our approach resulted in a more relevant AOP network for transcriptomics-based assessment of KE perturbation. These findings show molecular perturbation rather than direct proof of KE activation or causal progression through an AOP. When validated on larger and independent datasets, such networks will support mechanistic interpretation of transcriptomics data in chemical safety assessment.

papers.title: RNA evidence supports clinical stage antibody drug targets in oncology
papers.abstract: Background: The selection of efficacious and safe antibody-based oncology targets depends on tumor specificity and normal-tissue expression, and remains challenging. Bulk RNA-seq can identify tumor-enriched surface genes, but may obscure tumor specificity and normal-cell expression patterns that are relevant to the therapeutic window. We evaluated whether single-cell RNA-seq-derived expression features improve retrospective prioritization of clinically pursued antibody targets. Methods: We developed a bulk and single-cell RNA expression-based ranking framework across six solid tumor indications. 4,532 candidate surfaceome targets were scored using tumor Specificity, normal Safety, and blood Sink features derived from bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, or a combined modality. Ranking performance was evaluated against a curated validation set of tumor-associated antibody-based oncology targets using logistic regression, with odds ratios (ORs) reported per one-standard-deviation increase in score. Results: Higher Specificity scores were associated with clinical-stage target selection across all modalities. In cross-indication meta-analysis, single-cell Specificity showed higher ORs than bulk Specificity across clinical phase thresholds, including Phase [≥] 1 (OR 2.56 versus 1.81), Phase [≥] 2 (OR 2.77 versus 1.88), Phase [≥] 3 (OR 3.53 versus 2.04) and Approved targets (OR 3.51 versus 1.74). Combined bulk-and-single-cell Specificity showed intermediate enrichment. Specificity score alone did not consistently show a significant single-cell advantage over bulk in paired indication-level comparisons, except for Phase [≥] 3 targets. After adding normal-cell Safety and blood Sink features, the single-cell general score showed the strongest enrichment across thresholds (Phase [≥] 1 OR 3.61, Phase [≥] 2 OR 4.16, Phase [≥] 3 OR 5.57, and Approved targets OR 4.25). This general score also showed consistently significant single-cell advantage over bulk in paired indication-level comparisons. Safety contributed most strongly in the single-cell modality, increasing meta-analytic ORs by an average of ~36% across thresholds compared to Specificity alone. Performance varied by indication, with breast cancer showing weaker Specificity-based enrichment. Conclusion: Expression-derived ranking features are retrospectively enriched among clinically pursued tumor-associated antibody targets. Single-cell evidence is most informative when tumor Specificity is combined with normal-cell Safety information, supporting its use as an interpretable component of early antibody target prioritization. These findings are in alignment with recent evidence that single-cell RNA-based cell-type specificity supports clinical-stage targets and demonstrate that expression-driven ranking can systematically recover clinically relevant oncology targets.

papers.title: Hubness and local scaling in paired T cell receptor distance spaces
papers.abstract: Nearest-neighbour retrieval in T cell receptor distance spaces is uneven: some receptors enter many neighbour lists while others enter none. We quantified this hubness in paired variable-domain distances and evaluated local scaling as a post-processing correction. Across ITRAP-filtered dextramers, VDJdb and McPAS-TCR, the skewness of the ten-neighbour occurrence count was 1.26 to 1.50. Local scaling reduced it to 0.13 to 0.31. Under a diagnostic restriction requiring different V families on both chains, macro retrieval gain increased by 0.1418 on VDJdb (95% hierarchical bootstrap interval 0.0079 to 0.3016). The same untuned correction gave a gain of 0.1185 on the held-out IMMREP25 corpus (0.0040 to 0.2477). On IMMREP22, mean micro-AUC increased from 0.8091 to 0.8394, with improvement on 14 of 17 epitopes (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.0026). Gains for CDR3 edit distance and SCEPTR had the same direction but were not significant separately. The benefit has narrow boundaries. CDR3 length alone recovered approximately one-third to three-fifths of it. Eight corrections failed to give reproducible gains on deduplicated beta-only receptors in the two principal corpora. Unrestricted retrieval did not yield a gain surviving the declared multiplicity corrections. Directly penalizing neighbour occurrence was harmful, and clustering results depended on partition granularity. Hubness reduction and specificity retrieval are therefore distinct outcomes. These findings support reporting hubness alongside retrieval accuracy and testing local scaling within paired-domain evaluations; they do not establish a universal correction or an absolute benchmark ranking.

papers.title: Reciprocal effective conductance-based inference of protein-protein relationships delineates protein network hubs and macromolecular properties
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) are fundamental to the regulation and function of all cellular processes, yet our current understanding of the human interactome is limited by the specific PPI-related experiments performed to date. Moreover, whereas proteins with minimal research interest may have relatively few interaction-probing studies, other factors such as cancer related proteins are frequently represented in PPI studies, producing a highly uneven bias across current PPI data. Here, we apply effective conductance - a concept from circuit theory - to infer proximity relationships across all individual protein pairs on the basis of 1.2 million reported human PPI observations. Using a reciprocal analysis framework built on effective conductance, we identify statistically meaningful interactions within the network while otherwise filtering nonrelevant associations that are abundant in proteins with strong popularity bias. While this approach helps clarify the structural and functional properties of both minimally and maximally connected proteins, we further compute an interaction index between all macromolecular, multi-subunit complexes based on underlying protein-protein conductance scores. Leveraging this framework, which we name CoBRAA (Conductance-Based Reciprocal Association Analysis), we highlight unexpected findings, such as evidence that DNA-dependent RNA polymerase I, II, and III are characterized by surprisingly pervasive cross-complex interactions between enzyme-specific subunits, suggesting a potential for crosstalk between all three RNA polymerases. We further introduce CoBRAA as an open-access research tool that enables custom, user-specified exploration of both protein- and macromolecular-level interactions. We expect this resource to facilitate broader investigation and hypothesis generation across a wide range of proteins, pathways, and macromolecular systems.

papers.title: A split-control criterion for few-shot adaptation in single-cell perturbation prediction
papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation can help or harm single-cell perturbation prediction, but conventional evaluation shares a control estimate between calibration responses and held-out targets. We show how methods carry control error into their predictions and derive its contribution to score inflation. Nested control-depth experiments support inverse-depth scaling of inner-product inflation; correlation inflation also depends on the control noise-to-signal ratio. Independent-control scoring changed the rank of 40 of 52 configuration-dataset entries. We introduce SafeDelta, a split-control criterion that uses calibration data to decide whether to adapt. Across six datasets, mean gated gain was non-negative under the original two-control evaluation. On a deep plate, fixed predictions and decisions retained positive mean gains under three additional independent control references. The same reproducibility principle identified a fibrosis programme that localises to scar in human liver. These results inform adaptation decisions and control-depth planning.

papers.title: ScreenDMT reveals metabolites replicably associated with sleep disorders across three human cohorts
papers.abstract: The robust replication of scientific findings across independent studies is essential, yet it remains challenging in high-dimensional biological datasets. A critical aspect of true replication requires detecting not only the repeated presence but also the consistent direction of an effect. Traditional methods for evaluating replication often ignore effect directionality or lack adequate statistical power when adjusting for multiple comparisons. To address this, we extend the directional MaxP test (DMT) and our screening-integrated procedure, ScreenDMT, to evaluate directional replication across an arbitrary number of independent studies. We mathematically prove ScreenDMT's validity for an arbitrary number of studies when the studies' sample sizes grow unbounded. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate that ScreenDMT effectively controls error rates, such as the false discovery rate (FDR), in finite sample sizes and yields higher statistical power than competing methods especially for three studies. We applied the extended ScreenDMT to untargeted blood metabolomics profiles across three diverse human cohorts - ARIC (N=1,337), MESA (N=1,874), and HCHS/SOL (N=6,180) - to discover replicable biomarkers for dichotomous insomnia, long sleep, short sleep, and excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS). We found low levels of cortisol to be replicably associated with EDS, and high levels of n-formylmethionine to be associated with long sleep. Furthermore, directional pathway analysis revealed that low levels of xanthine metabolites are replicably associated with insomnia. These convergent findings validate ScreenDMT as a powerful methodology for simultaneous multi-cohort replication and offer robust insights into the metabolic signatures underlying sleep disorders across diverse populations.

papers.title: Towards Robust Automated Mouse Scratching Behavior Detection for Itch Research
papers.abstract: Automated detection of mouse scratching behavior could reduce manual annotation and is essential for preclinical itch research. However, robust performance across laboratories remains a challenge for current methods. We present Scratch-AID+, a framework dedicated to automated mouse scratching detection, including a diverse and progressive set of approaches: classic ResNet-based detectors, task-adaptive fine-tuning of video foundation models, and in-context learning with advanced multimodal large language models. To simulate real-world use cases, we benchmark on a public dataset and utilize additional cross-laboratory video recordings for independent testing. We find that classic baselines suffered severe performance degradation on external data under the realistic setting with sparse scratching events. In contrast, fine-tuned video foundation models successfully bridged this generalizability gap, achieving significantly better detection performance. Furthermore, frozen multimodal large language models demonstrated promising out-of-the-box ability using only few-shot demonstrations. We also examined the effects of different video preprocessing strategies. Our findings highlight the improved performance and generalizability of the adapted foundation models for automated scratching behavior analysis and shed light on the real-world deployment of such detectors. Our code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/scratch aid-plus/.

papers.title: VirtualSkin integrates skin-cell identity with intervention-response prediction
papers.abstract: Human skin atlases resolve a diverse set of cellular states, yet connecting these states to their responses to intervention remains difficult across independently sampled tissues. Here we present VirtualSkin, a cell language model that aligns skin transcriptomes with biological descriptions and supports intervention conditioned response prediction. We evaluated the model across independent atlas, disease, anatomical and perturbation cohorts, with donors, studies and perturbations withheld according to the experimental design. VirtualSkin improved inflammatory skin annotation by 0.056 macro F1 points and cell text retrieval by 0.12 Recall@10 points relative to the strongest corresponding comparators. The representation retained cell identity during study integration and transferred across ageing, systemic sclerosis, lymphoma and anatomical sites. Across five intervention cohorts, response prediction improved by 0.03 0.09 response-score points, with agreement at the levels of gene expression change, gene recovery and transcriptional programs. Paired tissue trajectories provided a complementary assessment in two donors per intervention. Component ablations and pairing controls localized the predictive contributions, while uncertainty estimates supported selective prediction under distribution shift. These results connect skin-cell recognition to intervention response prediction within a common evaluation framework and define the conditions under which predictions can inform experimental prioritization.

papers.title: Deep-learning-driven tumor microenvironment profiling improves immunotherapy response prediction
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy has transformed the management of many cancers, such as clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), yet durable clinical benefit is achieved in only a subset of patients. Immunotherapy outcomes are governed by the multicellular tumor microenvironment (TME), through the structured and directional interplay of regulatory programs and ligand-receptor communications. Yet most existing methods for immunotherapy response prediction rely on independent signatures or cell types and fail to model the structured and directional signaling network within the TME. To address this gap, we introduce EcoNet, a computational framework that first models ecosystems consisting of co-occurring cell states, then constructs intercellular and intracellular signaling networks based on the ecosystems, and applies a graph attention network to derive embeddings from the signaling network for immunotherapy response prediction. Pretrained on 2,532 pan-cancer immunotherapy samples across multiple cohorts, EcoNet outperformed existing prediction methods by 7.5-19.9% and marker-based signatures by 4.4-21.2% in AUC, and its high-attention genes were enriched among those required for T-cell-mediated tumor killing in an independent CRISPR screen; applied to ccRCC with disease-specific fine-tuning, it stratified an independent ccRCC cohort by clinical outcome (P=0.024). Biologically, high-attention genes capture an interferon-responsive program that enhances antigen presentation and immune infiltration. To validate these findings, we curated a ccRCC clinical cohort profiled with CosMx single-cell spatial transcriptomics (46 samples, ~450,000 cells) and found the response-associated TME configuration identified by EcoNet localized to immune-enriched niches, supporting the response stratification. These results establish EcoNet as a generalizable framework for TME-informed therapeutic response prediction, readily extensible to other cancer types and therapeutic contexts.

papers.title: A versatile set of computational tools for inference of genetic ancestry from human molecular data
papers.abstract: Molecular properties of human diseases and conditions often exhibit dependence on the genetic ancestry of the donor. In order to make more human molecular data available for ancestry-informed research, we developed a set of software tools termed Robust Ancestry Inference using Data Synthesis (RAIDS) for inference of genetic ancestry from sequence data that pose challenges to genotyping. Here we describe a recent expansion and refinement of RAIDS, applicable to nucleic-acid sequence data resultant from a broad range of experimental strategies. These strategies currently include whole-genome, whole-exome, and targeted gene panel sequencing, RNA-Seq, including single-cell RNA-Seq, chromatin-accessibility (ATAC-Seq), and protein-binding (ChIP-Seq) assays. RAIDS inferential tools perform robustly in the presence of somatic nucleic-acid alterations caused by cancer and under the conditions of extreme non-uniformity of sequence read coverage, yielding both global ancestry and ancestral admixtures of the donor. RAIDS is available as an eponymous Bioconductor package.

papers.title: Imputing relative abundances via Gaussian random fields
papers.abstract: Longitudinal studies with human participants frequently face the challenge of missing samples, which lead to incomplete trajectories of participant biomarkers and a reduction in data size. Existing approaches focus on single-variable imputation or model features one at a time, while neural networks typically require a large number of parameters and substantial training data. To address these challenges, we present an explainable model for multiple imputation of compositional samples based on a Gaussian random field (GRF). The model is specifically designed for longitudinal data: it incorporates participant-specific information and accounts for both temporal dependence across repeated observations and within-sample correlations, while using a moderate number of parameters. By coupling the GRF with sparse activation functions, the framework outputs sum-constrained compositions and explicitly models zero inflation. Under the Aitchison and Jensen--Shannon distances, our framework achieves imputation accuracy comparable to that of an observation-carrying baseline, while overcoming its static nature by modeling temporal trajectories and multivariate correlations. The resulting multiple imputations allow us to reconstruct complete datasets for downstream analysis and uncertainty quantification. We demonstrate the practical utility of our framework on gut microbiome datasets, restoring incomplete time series and achieving a balanced accuracy of 0.72 in predicting food allergy in infants (sensitivity 0.8) and of 0.64 in forecasting postpartum depression.

papers.title: BioMod: Biological Module Tokenization for Single-Cell Foundation Modeling
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models typically represent cells as flat sequences of individual genes, requiring higher-order biological organization to be inferred implicitly from sparse expression profiles. Similar to the evolution from character-level to semantic tokenization in natural language processing,we hypothesize that cellular states can be more efficiently represented using biologically meaningful intermediate units. Here we present BioMod, a 50-million-parameter single-cell foundation model that introduces biological modules as representation units between genes and cells. BioMod constructs an overlapping vocabulary of 660 biological modules derived from curated pathways and data-driven gene programs, replacing thousands of gene-level inputs with compact module representations. Pretrained on approximately 73 million human cells using high-ratio module masking with an asymmetric decoder, BioMod achieves state-of-the-art performance across cell-type annotation, zero-shot batch integration, perturbation-response prediction and drug-response forecasting while maintaining a compact architecture that enables efficient inference on a single GPU. Module-level analyses further demonstrate that BioMod captures biologically meaningful cellular programs and preserves pathway-level organization.

papers.title: Do LLM Proposers Improve Budgeted Search for Ionizable Lipids?
papers.abstract: Efficient lipid design under limited experimental budgets is a central challenge in computational chemistry and drug discovery. We introduce LEAF (Lipid Evolutionary Adaptive Framework), a matched-budget protocol for testing whether language-model proposers improve combinatorial molecular search relative to classical baselines. The study uses a 30,044-candidate ionizable-lipid space, a frozen Gaussian-process oracle fitted to experimental potency labels, and a separate active-learning surrogate. Four language models evaluated over eight seeds and three splits show no significant improvement over genetic-algorithm or random-search baselines. For Llama 8B, 79.1% of acquisition-selected queries repeat previously evaluated archive members. Removing duplicates reduces the performance gap on some splits but increases proposal cost and can prevent budget exhaustion. Larger models reduce duplication without establishing superiority or equivalence. Exploratory scored prompts and stricter novelty controls yield positive median differences against the genetic algorithm, yet wide intervals and shared-seed dependence preclude stronger conclusions. A validated single-assay reanalysis preserves the chemotype-cold deficit at a smaller numerical scale, and exploratory expected hypervolume improvement does not reverse the result. Follow-up checks address whether proposers genuinely use injected evidence. These checks include a zero-shot leakage probe, rank-only and chain-of-thought-rationale prompts, a score-shuffle perturbation, an evidence-conflict probe, and a genuine reasoning-mode proposer. They show measurable engagement with supplied information without a corresponding performance gain. LEAF isolates proposal quality as the experimental variable and documents a concrete failure mode of zero-shot LLM proposers under controlled budgets.

papers.title: Optimizing copy number profiles for tumor cell phylogeny inference from low-coverage single-cell sequencing data
papers.abstract: Motivation: Accurate reconstruction of tumor cell phylogenies is crucial for understanding cancer evolutionary dynamics, inferring intra-tumor heterogeneity, and designing effective and personalized cancer treatment strategies. One of the most promising and cost-effective approaches for reconstructing tumor phylogenies for large numbers of cells is to use copy number alteration (CNA) data obtained from low-coverage single-cell DNA sequencing of sampled tumor cells. However, error and uncertainty in inferred copy number profiles (CNPs), resulting from low sequence coverage, can have a drastic negative effect on the reconstruction accuracy of tumor cell phylogenies. Results: In this work, we show that careful selection of bin size, a critical tuning parameter for inferring CNPs, is necessary to maximize the accuracy of tumor cell phylogeny inference. Specifically, we (i) use three previously published low-coverage single-cell DNA sequencing datasets from real tumors to demonstrate that even small changes in bin size can have a drastic impact on downstream tumor phylogeny reconstruction, (ii) show that this effect persists even when using simulated low-coverage datasets generated under idealized conditions with minimal noise, and (iii) propose a simple computational approach to select bin sizes that maximize tumor phylogeny accuracy. Our experiments span a wide range of bin sizes and account for the impact of various factors including coverage-level, phylogeny reconstruction method, and CNP inference method, and explicitly account for phylogenetic reconstruction uncertainty. Our evaluation of the proposed computational approach for bin size selection shows that it can significantly improve tumor cell phylogeny reconstruction accuracy compared to baseline methods. Availability: Freely available from https://github.com/Tanveer14/BinSelector.

papers.title: Efficient approximate Bayesian inference for large, heterogeneous biological datasets
papers.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) offers a route to connect biological data with mechanistic models. At the frontier of biology, datasets continue to grow in scale and richness, and increasingly record heterogeneity between individual observations that a mechanistic model can take into account. Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) remains a popular approach to SBI due to its ease of use, but incorporating this heterogeneity often requires a separate simulation of each observation, which is prohibitively expensive at scale. A previously proposed technique, minibatch Sequential Monte Carlo ABC (SMC ABC), reduces this cost by simulating a fixed-size random subset of observations for each proposal, at the price of sampling noise that limits precision. Here, we present an adaptive minibatch approach that uses small batches during early exploration and increases the batch size as the posterior is refined. The adaptive batch size is set by the target precision and does not grow with the size of the dataset, so the savings over full-data SMC ABC increase for larger datasets. We demonstrate the method on synthetic biological models and on real single-cell gene-expression data that vary in scale and type of heterogeneity, including cell geometry and initial condition. In each case, the adaptive scheme obtains posteriors close to those of full-data SMC ABC at a fraction of the cost. Altogether, adaptive minibatching improves the tradeoff between speed and precision in SMC ABC and opens the door to mechanistic inference on large, heterogeneous biological datasets.

papers.title: Surrogate variables and the risk of overfitting in neuropsychiatric gene expression analyses
papers.abstract: The reproducibility crisis in biomedical research calls for re-evaluation of how common analytic approaches affect results. One such approach, surrogate variable analysis (SVA), is widely used to adjust for unmeasured drivers of variation in transcriptomic differential expression analyses. We systematically quantified the impact of SVA using synthetic data with known ground truth and fourteen brain RNA-seq and microarray datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and Parkinson's disease. In synthetic data, SVA usage frequently led to high false positive rates. This issue was not revealed by standard diagnostics nor resolved by strategies such as maximizing cross-dataset signal correlation. In real data, using SVA reduced cross-cohort reproducibility of differential expression signatures regardless of the number of surrogate variables included. These findings show that SVA risks inducing overfitting at realistic signal levels, advocating for a cautious, case-by-case application, with a preference for modeling known covariates.

papers.title: scGSCA: gene-set differential co-expression analysis for single-cell RNA sequencing data
papers.abstract: Understanding disease-associated pathway coordination requires distinguishing phenotype-related co-expression changes from differences across cellular contexts while accounting for cells sampled from the same subject. Bulk gene-set co-expression methods do not directly address the sparse counts, single-cell distributional noise, subject-level dependence, and cell-type heterogeneity of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. We developed single-cell gene-set co-expression analysis (scGSCA), a framework for pathway-level differential co-expression analysis in scRNA-seq data. scGSCA fits gene-wise zero-inflated negative binomial mixed models with subject-level random effects and computes gene-set co-expression statistics from quantile residual correlations. It provides an overall differential gene-set co-expression analysis and an interaction test to assess whether the co-expression pattern between two cell types varies by sample phenotype. We applied scGSCA to tumor-normal gastric, breast-subtype, and lung-skin comparisons with matched bulk and scRNA-seq data. The overall test identified signals not captured in bulk analysis, including Axon guidance in gastric cancer and estrogen-response, IL6-JAK-STAT3, and TNF/NF-{kappa}B pathways in breast cancer. The interaction test further identified co-expression contrasts across cell types. scGSCA extends gene-set co-expression analysis to single-cell data while retaining subject-level structure and cell-type-specific context. scGSCA is freely available as an open-source R package.

papers.title: CLARA: Compound Library Active Learning with Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: Batch active learning for ligand discovery requires a recurring decision about whether to exploit high predicted affinity, reduce model uncertainty, or broaden chemical coverage. We test whether a language model can make this strategy-level decision while candidate ranking and label revelation remain controlled by a deterministic Gaussian-process environment. Across four protein targets, ten paired seeds, and a 360-compound assay budget, a GPT-5.6 Sol agent outperformed random sampling in all 40 matched campaigns. Its final top-2% recall was 0.412 on D2R, 0.374 on Mpro, 0.448 on TYK2, and 0.683 on USP7. It was statistically tied with the strongest fixed policy on Mpro and USP7 but underperformed target-specific leaders on D2R and TYK2. The agent shifted from exploration-oriented early batches toward exploitation and produced 686 testable threshold claims with an 86.3% atomic success rate, although 19.8% of forecasts were not numerically scorable. In 200 prespecified information-ablation campaigns, removing uncertainty, diversity, or memory caused only small endpoint changes, while shuffling explanatory evidence reproduced the full allocation path in 39 of 40 paired campaigns. A deterministic 80% availability constraint reduced recall on every target but preserved the target-dependent pattern of wins and losses. These results support language-model strategy control as a feasible and auditable layer.

papers.title: Structure-Based Drug Design of Novel Inhibitors Targeting the Thiamine Biosynthesis Pathway in Bacteria
papers.abstract: Current generation antibiotics are limited by poor target selectivity and are often mismanaged, leading to widespread antimicrobial resistance. The bacterial thiamine biosynthesis pathway offers compelling alternative since it is highly essential for bacterial survival and yet absent in humans. Genetic perturbations within pathway lead to documented auxotrophy and virulence defects, indicating low mutational tolerance within this pathway. Thiamine phosphate synthase is a key bottleneck enzyme performing the crucial role of coupling thiazole and pyrimidine moieties to form thiamine monophosphate. To develop a suitable inhibitor against it, a structure-based drug design pipeline was implemented. High-throughput virtual screening of nearly 1.5 million molecules provided sufficient exploration of chemical space. Further, R-group substitution was utilized for lead optimization. Structure-Activity Relationship analysis upon molecular mutants reveals patterns among R-group interactions to catalytic residues across various scaffolds. Additionally, ADMET screening and validation using molecular dynamics simulations resulted in a potent orally bioavailable broad-spectrum bactericidal molecule.

papers.title: High-performance xenograft read-sorting for DNA methylation analysis
papers.abstract: Xenograft sorting tools separate sequenced DNA reads by species. We have enhanced the computational method and tool Xengsort to enable efficient epigenetic profiling of patient-derived xenograft models; it now supports cytosine-converted whole genome or reduced-representation data. Benchmarking Xengsort against several established methods (ICRG, bamcmp, XenofilteR) revealed consistently high accuracy across tools, but Xengsort outperformed the other tools in computational efficiency due to its alignment-free design.

papers.title: Probing isn't Causality in Molecular Models
papers.abstract: Linear probes establish whether a chemical variable can be recovered from a molecular representation; they do not establish how that variable contributes to subsequent predictions. We replace a concept-associated scalar component at an intermediate block and measure the change through a separately fitted downstream outcome readout. Comparisons with random directions and architecture-matched random encoders distinguish recoverability, intervention selectivity, and a pretraining-associated selectivity advantage. In Uni-Mol, block-12 total-distortion edits predict the observed energy-change sign for 97.6% of held-out pairs, with Spearman $rho=0.787$. Structure-clustered intervals for the primary direction and encoder contrasts exclude zero. A stricter 20-direction sensitivity analysis does not survive correction across six cells. A post-review analysis finds substantial concept--outcome alignment; intervention effects persist after removal of the same-block outcome direction, but this does not establish that subsequent encoder computation is necessary. In MolCLR, pretraining improves dipole recovery by $0.080,R^2$, whereas concept-minus-random sign-accuracy contrasts are $0.029$ and $-0.015$ at the two tested blocks. Their paired uncertainty is unresolved, so they do not establish an absence of selective effects. We propose an operational evidence ladder whose conclusions are conditional on the concept, intervention, control family, and fitted readout.

papers.title: UPLiFT: Uncertainty Parameterized Activation for Lightweight Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Learned protein representations contribute to the broad utility of pretrained protein language models (PLMs), often enhanced by task-specific fine-tuning where parameter-efficient techniques are imperative due to large network size. Our work takes an orthogonal approach to such fine-tuning: rather than optimizing the network weights, we formulate adaptation as an optimization task over the parameterized activation space. Motivated by the prior work on curvature-tuning, we propose UPLiFT, Uncertainty Parameterized activation for Lightweight Fine-Tuning, with enhanced adaptation capacity when the underlying model--whether pretrained or randomly initialized--remains fixed, for significantly improved parameter efficiency. Furthermore, its learnable non-linearity naturally allows to model uncertainty over the activation space through fine-tuning in a variational inference framework. Evaluation across multiple protein datasets shows that UPLiFT performs competitively while requiring 3-11x fewer trainable parameters than weight-only adaptations. Bayesian UPLiFT further improves calibration while largely preserving the predictive performance of deterministically fine-tuned models. The narrow predictive performance margin with the low-rank adaptation baseline in residue-level tasks highlights the potential of our proposed approach as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique for PLM-based predictors.

papers.title: phyloDS: phylogeny-aware differential splicing across species, beyond reference annotations
papers.abstract: Alternative splicing diverges rapidly between species, yet its comparative analysis lags far behind that of gene expression: junction orthology is defined on a single reference genome, species are treated as independent samples, and detected shifts are rarely grounded in sequence-level evidence. We present phyloDS, an RNA-seq--driven framework that resolves all three limitations. phyloDS defines orthologous splice junctions on multiple sequence alignments of one-to-one orthologous genes, tests their differential usage with a regularized Ornstein--Uhlenbeck model, and cross-validates detected shifts against splice-site predictions made from genomic sequence alone. Applied to primate brain and rodent heart transcriptomes, phyloDS recovered up to 2.9-fold more shared orthologous splice junctions than a reference-based strategy and kept type~I error near nominal where competing methods inflate it more than two-fold. It identified 234 and 502 differentially used orthologous splice junctions in hominoids and mole-rats (86 and 141 unannotated), revealing a mitochondrial and contractile splicing signature in mole-rats.

papers.title: Application of Bayesian-Derived Gene Interaction Network and Subnetwork for Classification of Idiopathic Parkinson Disease with Biomarkers
papers.abstract: Given the expenses associated with Parkinson Disease (PD), it is imperative to develop a method for accurate diagnosis before emergence of motor symptoms. While there are tests that can measure early onset of PD, these tests still rely on subjective input from patients and can thus be biased. Factors influencing their accuracy include environmental agents such as education and culture. Thus, blood-based transcriptomic signatures are a promising direction for biomarkers in PD that are minimally invasive and more objective than clinical evaluation. In this paper, we analyzed gene expression from the PPMI cohort. Using a Bayesian framework, a gene interaction network was constructed to enhance differential expressed genes (DEG) analysis through signal diffusion. In tandem with clinical traits, 13 genes were selected for optimal discrimination using a random forest model. Within the holdout test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.972, outperforming contemporary models. The model performance demonstrates the potential of using blood-based transcriptomics to enhance clinical diagnosis of PD. Other genes recovered by network diffusion but missed by traditional DEG analysis are already validated as potential biomarkers in contemporary PD research. By combining transcriptomic signatures with clinical evaluation, accurate diagnosis of PD can happen before the major destruction of dopaminergic neurons, which is critical for effective intervention and treatment.

papers.title: AnnZarro: scalable, interactive exploration of cell-by-cell and gene-by-gene relationships in single-cell data
papers.abstract: Cell-by-cell and gene-by-gene relationships, such as kernels and correlations, shape most single-cell analyses but are rarely inspected directly due to a lack of visualization tools that display them. AnnZarro is a point-and-click browser viewer that shows these matrices linked to an AnnData object's cells x genes data. Using AnnZarro, experimental biologists can explore data without code and computational biologists can probe the relationships behind their analyses. One focused cell and one focused gene drive every panel. Clicking a cell paints its row of any cell-by-cell matrix over an embedding or spatial coordinates; clicking a gene paints its row of any gene-by-gene matrix over a gene plot such as a volcano. The focus also links genes to the cells where they change, and cells to the genes that distinguish them. AnnZarro reads only the matrix rows and columns each panel displays from zarr stores and hence users can explore matrices far larger than memory on a laptop or a shared server. Large datasets open on a reproducible subset, and users step through the remaining cells in parts. On a laptop, a 100,000-cell part of Tahoe-100M opens in 4 s and stays interactive. With the subset switched off, AnnZarro draws all 95.6 million cells in one plot in about 5 to 7 s. This tutorial prepares a dataset with Kompot differential abundance and expression, a diffusion kernel and gene correlations, then explores it in six worked examples.
